Cleopatra

Saara El-Arifi, Simona Berlovan (Translator)

3.90
19,752 ratings3,783 reviews
Rate this book
Această poveste nu este despre cum am murit, ci despre cum am trăit.
Eu, Cleopatra cea adevărată.
Istoricii mi-au rostit numele ca pe o insultă, pentru că bărbații nu au acceptat niciodată să fie conduși de o femeie puternică. Au preferat să spună că am sedus imperii, nu că le-am înțeles.
Dramaturgii m-au numit vrăjitoare, pentru că nu au găsit alt cuvânt pentru limba zeilor pe care am învățat-o. Am vorbit greaca, egipteana, latina, limbile Orientului. Am știut să mă adresez poporului pe limba lui, lucru pe care puțini dintre înaintașii mei l-au făcut.
Poeții au cântat despre setea mea de sânge, de parcă nu orice mamă ar da dovadă de cruzime pentru a-și proteja copiii. Au uitat foametea pe care am oprit-o deschizând grânarele și datoriile pe care le-am renegociat. Au uitat că un tron nu este un jilț de aur, ci o povară care îți apasă umerii zi și noapte.
Preoții au spus că sunt o anomalie pe tronul Egiptului, doar pentru că sunt femeie. Dar eu am fost crescută să fiu deopotrivă zeu și conducător. Am purtat pe frunte uraeusul nu ca podoabă, ci ca responsabilitate. Am știut că fiecare inundație a Nilului, fiecare zvon din Alexandria, fiecare mișcare a Romei îmi poate clătina țara.
Adevărul este că o femeie care gândește strategic este întotdeauna periculoasă pentru cei care vor să o reducă la tăcere.
Cleopatra... acesta este numele meu. Și aceasta este prima carte din lume prin care îmi pot spune povestea. Istoria nu m-a lăsat să fac asta, dar acum nu mă mai poate ignora.
Nimeni nu știe cine am fost cu adevărat. Până acum.

About the author

Saara El-Arifi

14 books3,988 followers
Saara El-Arifi is the Sunday Times bestselling author of The Ending Fire Trilogy
and the Faebound Trilogy.

El-Arifi knew she was a storyteller from the moment she told her first lie. Over the years, she has perfected her tall tales into epic ones. She has lived in many countries, had many jobs, and owned many more cats. After a decade of working in marketing and communications, she returned to academia to complete a master’s degree in African studies alongside her writing career. She currently resides in London as a full-time procrastinator.

February 24, 2026
If you have ever side eyed Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights casting choices for Heathcliff and thought but “why are you white” (omg Karen you can't just ask people why they're white), then you may feel similarly about 1963 Hollywood’s expensive fanfiction of Cleopatra starring Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton.

But to be clear, this is so much much much more than about Cleo’s skin shade and cultural origin.

If you're seeking a more emotionally intelligent, more historically grounded account of Cleo*, I would highly recommend checking out Saara El-Arifi’s Cleopatra. Because it’s crystal clear to me that this author’s version of Cleopatra is doing a lot more than interpreting numerous historical texts to bring to us a more authentic memoir-style historical fiction-biography (with mythological fantasy elements) of one of the most famous women in classical antiquity.

It’s also dismantling and decentring the historical male gaze which has been shaped by Roman propaganda (for example Cicero or Boccaccio). In other words, just men calling a strong intelligent political leader who happens to be a woman, “seductress, witch, whore, villain.”

It's no secret that history is written by the victors but did you know that in some cases it's cultivated and cherrypicked by misogynists? Just saying. We’re all tired.

For example, Boccaccio’s account of Cleopatra’s early reign condemns her sexuality, portrays Cleopatra as a tyrant rather than a queen by birthright, and distorts her narrative to show Cleopatra gaining power by taking it from men, through seduction and tyranny. (Source)

Anyway, I can say this version of Cleopatra was a breath of fresh air, truly. El-Arifi keeps it real. She’s not framing Cleopatra as some sort of great saintly feminist icon who has been wronged by men either. She’s portrayed with flaws, guilt and regrets. She makes mistakes, she’s cunning, strategic and ambitious. She acknowledges her own ruthlessness and cruelty that shape her story and doesn’t try to sugarcoat them. But the most important thing is, this version centres her story, from her life, to her loves and her losses with nuance, without pigeonholing her into a two dimensional archetype fashioned to soothe an insecure man’s fear of a powerful woman emasculating him. (Note: IMO, men with healthy masculinity are not threatened by strong, confident women).

*You can check the author’s notes to see what creative liberties she took if that’s something you’re interested in. There is also a good dash of mythological fantasy in the sense of Egyptian mythology’s gods and goddesses. And I think it was all done beautifully.

Anyways, enough emotional spiralling. The ending of this was poignant and breathtaking and I think someone was chopping onions nearby when I finished it. I thought this was going to be a four star read but I had to upgrade it to five by the end.

Highly recommend. Could someone please turn this into a film?

Thanks so much to HarperCollins UK and Netgalley for the ARC.

Between the unexpected loss of our sweetest girl, Lola 🐇, dealing with contractors and home renovations, and saying goodbye to two of our baby foster bunnies who were adopted, this past week has been overwhelming to say the least. Thankfully, I had this book to curl up with to help get me through a very stressful week.

“You know my name. But you do not know me.”

Cleopatra narrates the story in the first person, giving the novel an intimate feel, as though she is telling her story directly to the reader. The book is divided into three parts: The Witch, The Whore, and The Villain.

What I loved most about this book was the author’s choice to highlight the Egyptian queen’s intelligence, humanity, and loyalty rather than the seductress she has so often been reduced to throughout history. Did she have flaws? Absolutely. Did she make poor choices? Most definitely. But this narrative allows us to see her as so much more—a pharaoh, a mother, a sister, a friend, and a wife.

While I really enjoyed this one, two things kept it from being a five-star read for me. The first was a slow start, and the second was the often heavy-handed foreshadowing. Cleopatra frequently gives the reader clues about what is to come, which I felt took away some of the story’s mystique and mystery.

This was my first book by this author, but it definitely won’t be my last. I’m already looking forward to whatever she writes next. The story sent me on a deep dive into Cleopatra’s history and left me wanting to learn more about what became of her children. Highly recommend!

⭐️ 5 ⭐️ Witch. Whore. Villain.
In every tale there is a legend and a monster.

This is a tale about a life once lived full of curiosity and reflection, a story about a woman who’s captured everyone’s imagination. It’s about unwavering love and devotion, fragility of life and cultural legacy. It’s fierce, it’s vivid, it’s a complete stunner. It’s a book that leaves you sitting silently, thinking how even in death, a voice can never be silenced.

The retelling follows Cleopatras childhood and coming of age tale along with her rise to power. Much of what is know about Cleopatras life comes from Greco-Roman scholars, where she is perceived for what she was versus who she was. Much of what we know about her comes from records written by men, written and shaped by their beliefs and stereotypes. Since much of history is flawed, it’s very hard to imagine a concrete version of Cleopatra. Mainly known for her surpassing beauty and the first woman to rule Egypt in her own right, Cleopatra was often called the ‘golden-mouth’ for her eloquence, persuasion and intellectual skills. While she’s always portrayed as the essence of beauty, we often overlook how she stood tall in the face of tyranny and fought for justice.

Saara El-Arifi shakes that piece of history by writing a tale that adds more layers to Cleopatras life. She transports us to ancient Egypt, allowing us to see the vibrancy and beauty of ancient world through Cleopatras eyes. She brings her back to life with a captivating take on her life and love story, her journey to ascension, rule and eventually her death. El-Arifi takes us through sands of time in this powerful story of a woman who was viewed as a witch, whore and a villain by men in power. I’ve learned a lot from this historical retelling, facts that I never knew or heard of. I was immensely impressed with the pacing, magical elements and even how all the side characters carried a piece of their own history. I knew of her legacy, specifically what she was and how she was perceived but I never knew of who she was, her strengths and weaknesses, her fears. This was by far the best retelling of Cleopatra that I’ve ever read.



Thank you to NetGalley, Ballantine Books and the author Saara El-Arifi for sending me this eARC!

Death will silence me no longer.
This is not the story of how I died. But how I lived.

Historical fiction told from the perspective of Cleopatra herself memoir-style. As Pharaoh of Egypt. As a lover to two different infamous Roman consuls. As the femme fatale that led to Rome conquering Egypt.

"Some called me Queen, lover, Mama. Others called me witch, villain, whore. Each archetype is a brick that has raised me up like the great pyramids, further and further away from my humanity until I have become nothing more than a myth."

Queen | Lover | Mama

Pharaoh Cleopatra's first and greatest love was always Egypt.

Outside of Egypt, there were two men that equally captivated her heart at different points in time. First was Julius Caesar, the infamous Roman "dictator for life". Second, there was Marcus Antonius (better known as Mark Antony in history books), another Roman general whose heartwrenching love with Cleopatra spelled out both of their eventual doom.

Julius was a wizened elder that helped Cleopatra flourish as a pharaoh; they stimulated each other mentally as well as physically. Whereas Marcus was the man who helped Cleo blossom as a woman. Their love was the kind worth dying for.

"Antonius's laugh came to be like the sun, passionate and intense. Caesar's was always like the rain, exhilirating and pure. And as if I were a flower in bloom, both sustained me."

Two vastly different men, yet both went on to leave behind a remnant of themselves with her. Through a child(ren).

Witch | Villain | Whore

History is written by the victors, and though I know that this is a work of fiction, I can't help but wonder what our historians would have to say about Cleopatra had she not eventually lost out to Octavian. There's a line from this book that sums this up perfectly: "History is a disease. It masquerades as truth, but no one can replicate a moment in words alone."

As is the case with any strong and capable woman, there'll always be people trying to tear them down. Calling a strong political leader that just so happens to be a woman "witch, villain, or whore." Roman propaganda turned the prosperous Pharaoh of Egypt into a common whore that was out there bewitching their valiant general.

Am I saying that Cleopatra was without fault? Or someone who didn't kill innocents? Absolutely not. She herself admits to it. To protect her children. To protect Egypt. To save her own skin. Cleopatra sheds A LOT of blood.

It's obvious that this was a well-researched book even with its fantastical twists, and the final product excels all the more because of it! Cleopatra is a book I whole-heartedly recommend checking out; it's a vivid and dramatic tale that weaves its way through decades of rich Egyptian history through the eyes of one of the world's most notorious women!

October 10, 2025
How I wished to love this book more. It had all the ingredients to be extraordinary — a talented author with a track record of strong female leads, one of history’s most fascinating women at its centre, and a period brimming with intrigue and drama. Alas, it was not to be.

This novel offers a fictionalised account of the life and death of Cleopatra. It’s well-researched and occasionally engaging, blending elements of magic and romance into the mix. As a narrative summary of Cleopatra’s life, it succeeds: the author captures much of the allure and tragedy of this legendary figure, staying (mostly) true to known history.

But that’s where the praise ends. The book is, frankly, a mess — and I’m still surprised I managed to finish it. The greatest flaw lies in the portrayal of Cleopatra herself, which is inconsistent, shallow, and often unintentionally insulting. While we’ll never know the true nature of the real Cleopatra, it’s hard to imagine she was as foolish or incompetent as depicted here. I don’t believe the author intended to make her seem dim-witted, yet the result suggests poor judgment, zero leadership ability, and a blind hunger for power. It’s simply not a credible portrayal of a woman who ruled Egypt for years and captivated two of Rome’s most formidable leaders.

The writing doesn’t help. It veers between lazy and overwrought, with dialogue so clumsy it borders on parody. The author’s attempts at sounding profound only make things worse — the pompous sentences are almost painful (“for I know how it feels to have your life reduced to actions and assumptions”). Coming from a writer capable of much better, this is baffling.

Then there’s the romance — and it’s downright offensive. I understand that romantasy sells, but it still needs to be written well. The endless scenes of love-talk and love-making between Cleopatra and her lovers feel contrived, forced, and entirely devoid of authenticity or emotional truth.

I also personally really disliked the constant foreshadowing - with Cleopatra talking again and again to the reader telling them what's coming in a few pages. At a certain point it became infuriating.

Ultimately, the novel suffers from a lack of focus. It can’t decide whether it wants to be historical fiction, romance, or fantasy — and ends up failing on all counts.

I can’t recommend it to anyone, not even long-time fans of the author. A huge missed opportunity.

My thanks to NetGalley and the publisher for providing an early copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Mika

March 8, 2026
*I received an advance review copy for free, and I am leaving this review voluntarily.*

Quick Recommendation

Cleopatra by Saara El-Arifi is a re-telling of the Egyptian and Ptolemaic Queen Kleopatra VII. It focuses on her humanity, womenhood, friendships and power. A modern take that refuses to use the misogynistic undertones of the source material. This is not told in a way to objective Kleopatra or make her appear as the villain. It tells the story of a woman who tried to protect her family and friends, who was merciless to those who wronged her and who loved Egypt and her people deeply.

While it's religious with a touch of magical realism it also includes political intrigues, love and war.
While it takes liberties, most of the events included in this re-telling are historically accurate.

This novel highlights how patriarchal systems and hearsay distorted the portrayal of Kleopatra as a woman and as a ruler.

It's for those who want to read Egyptian mythology and for those who want to read a book where the woman is the one in power.

Pacing

It started too slow and the ending felt rushed and abrupt. The start could have been faster and the ending could have had more chapters to make it more steady. No complaints about the middle part.

Writing Style

The story is told in first-person narration where Kleopatra reflects back on her life after her death. Sometimes she foreshadows upcoming events that might spoil the fun. I personally liked to know what might happen next and thought that her narrative voice was fresh and unique compared to the traditional texts about her.

Themes

Main themes
Leadership, loyalty vs disloyalty, friend vs foe, power (mortal and divine), betrayals and treasons, vengeance, political intrigues & alliances, love vs duty, patriarchal systems, societal expectations and roles, legacy, humanity and sibling rivalry.

Other themes
Women and motherhood, friendship, loneliness, afterlife, losses, sacrifices, resilience, survival, ambitions, grief, glory, pride, dignity, taking responsibilities and independence.

Characters

Kleopatra (Kleopatra VII Thea Neōtera Philopatōr Philopatris)
It was interesting getting to know Kleopatra. The more the story moved forward the more character traits of her were revealed. Some that I liked and some that I didn't. I was fond of her deep love towards Egypt, her people, her family and her friends. She was a very caring person which love was used to objective her as nothing but beauty and seduction. It was a shock for me to read a paragraph that quoted a historian that claimed that Kleopatra slept with 100+ men. That was exaggerated and there was no known evidence, so it was injustified for that historian to say that.

What I admired about her was her deep belief to the goddess Isis, whom she never stopped praying to. She might be cunning, merciless and ruthless but she is also loyal towards her people and the Gods who gifted her family divine blessings to wield their power. Her strategic thinking was often misinterpreted as weakness. She was smarter than most assumed, 'cause she was living a life where she worked behind-the-scenes—away from the public. She planned most of her political and strategic decisions in hiding. Not only did she operate in secret for plans but also to protect and help Egypt. Following her journey filled me with joy and anticipation as to what happens next.

Arsinoë IV
I disliked her quite a lot. Arsinoë took everything for granted and was asking for more than she deserved. She was an important portrayal of the sibling rivalry, which caused her own downfall. What made me so irritated about her was how she also caused the downfall of somebody else by influencing them badly. She was interesting as a sister to Kleopatra and her divine blessing, but except that I just wanted her to be gone.

Ptolemy XIII (Mikro) Theos Philopator
I liked him quite a lot. Some might disagree with me, but I think he was a victim. Ptolemy XIII got involved into something he wasn't supposed to way too quickly before he could fathom what was happening. I could understand his frustration and anger too well, but I hoped for him to appreciate the decision his sister chose for him. She just tried to protect him but he was too young to realise that.

Julius Caesar
While I can't belive that Caesar actually behaved that way, I was still charmed by his demeanour. He was a true gentleman who respected his woman and who was not easily angered. Quite the opposite—he was a thoughtful and assertive man. He was confident, not arrogant. He was curious, not nosy. He was generous not selfish. Caesar might not have been my favourite, but it was exciting to see where his journey led to.

Outroduction

Big thanks to NetGalley and Ballantine for providing me with the advanced reader copy of Cleopatra by Saara El-Arifi.

This was heart-wrenchingly beautiful?!

Cleopatra is always depicted as a temptress. An Empress, but also a poisoner, a snake - rather than a wife, a mother, a caring princess.
Cleopatra’s myth has permeated collective memory. Her story lives in the minds of many, far beyond what history has provided.

El-Arifi recounts a compassionate tale of a girl, a woman despised and used as propaganda. Instead of her political exploits, we read a story of love, sympathy, and internal strife.

You have tried to parse the tones of my skin and sift through the crimson rubies of my blood, upon which you weighed my worth.

This is truly a story told by Cleopatra. There are asides told to us as if from the beyond. Depending on your personal taste, this might grate on you: ‘as you will know’, footnotes, etc. However, this breaking of the fourth wall made it feel more intimate.

I was still very aware it was written by someone else as an interpretation, but I felt wrapped up in the Pharaoh’s story as Cleo.

She is humanised by her friendships and kindness. Her cruelty is put into context and her love is presented not as a spectacle, but something meaningful and hurtful.

But women have ever been defined by their affiliation with men.

Huge thanks to NetGalley and HarperCollins UK for the ARC!

🌟🌟🌟🌟/5

"That's the thing with stories: you must always know the story of the storyteller."

In 'Cleopatra', Saara el-Arifi peels away layers of propaganda and mythmaking in an attempt to humanize one of the most famous historical figures of all time. I'm fascinated with the life of Cleopatra and this just fed my obsession.

Here's everything I loved:
● The author's note was fantastic. Cleopatra's tale, like those of other women who dared to be ambitious, has been warped and twisted by male historians. In the author's note, Saara el-Arifi explains why her rendition is no less true than any of the others. Her approach really resonated with me and I'm glad the author's not was printed at the start of the book itself, since that really shaped my perspective.
● Cleopatra has assumed serval roles in her lifetime: the Pharaoh and the not-quite-goddess, the mother and the wife, the lover and the friend. el-Arifi reconciled these wonderfully. She isn't one-dimensional in any way, she isn't just an ambitious seductress or a ruthless villain: she's a woman who made mistakes, a woman who wanted more than what the world offered her and was willing to go to any lengths for it, but also a woman who loved deeply.
● The use of the setting and the time period was fabulous! I was utterly transported. el-Arifi brought the Alexandria's multicultural environment, customs of the ancient world, and so much more to life.
● I loved the way el-Arifi spun a tapestry of Cleopatra's life. Everything came together towards the end in a very satisfying way, despite the bit-too-rushed ending. I felt like I KNEW Cleopatra as I followed her through her triumphs and misfortunes.

What didn't quite work for me:
● In the book, Cleopatra directly addresses the reader and makes references to her own future or to her contemporaries' take on her tale. For instance, she'd say "I should have known...." or "Your poets say...". This narrative style didn't completely click with me.
● There is often a tension or a tautness to the narrative when a story heads towards its tragic ending. It plays a pretty big role in how hard-hitting the story ends up being. The ending was a bit too rushed for me to feel that.

I'm not quite sure how I feel about the epilogue. It made perfect sense but at the same time, none at all. But overall, I'd say that this is a book worth reading, especially if you've ever wondered how Cleopatra would tell her tale on her own terms or just...been obsessed with ancient Egypt! Although I was disappointed by 'Faebound', Saara el-Arifi's romantasy series starter, Cleopatra was a hit. I will eagerly anticipate whatever works of historical fiction she has in store! Off I go to read Stacy Schiff's biography of Cleopatra!

I will not be led in triumph, I vowed.

At the age of eighteen, Cleopatra VII was crowned leader of Egypt.

Who was she?

Many have tried to tell us her story including Shakespeare and Elizabeth Taylor.

Here is what I liked about this new title by Saara ElArifi:

👸The crown was thrust upon her before she was given a gifting by one of Egypt's gods. In desperation she fashioned herself into a healer. Cleopatra claimed Isis as her own. Some whispered WITCH of her.

💏She was the mother of four children. One by Julius Caesar and three by Marus Antony. Her enemies labeled her a WHORE behind her back, but she was married to both under Egypt's laws. Rome begged to differ and considered them illegitimate.

🐊When Octavian refuses to recognize Cleopatra's children as heirs to the power of Rome, she becomes a VILLAIN and fights back. This third section ends with a flourish and is a more hopeful future for this queen than many have given her.

👑The opulent cover of this new title is the perfect foil for the story inside. Cleopatra tells her own story and we are there with her. Such a strong sense of place and time!

This will be my first of two Cleopatra books this spring. Marie Benedicts Daughter of Egypt is coming out this year as well. The writing in this one veered into romantasy territory and I struggled to connect at times. Others have been much more complimentary and I encourage checking out other reviews.

Thank you to Ballantine Books and Edelweiss+ for a DRC in exchange for an honest review. This title will be available on February 24, 2026.

There is no slow introduction to this novel. At the very beginning Cleopatra is thrown into a new chapter of her life. Her father has died, and she is his heir.

I enjoyed that this did not get too caught up in explaining the grand events, and kept itself rooted in the characters. It also made them feel different enough, with different customs and traditions and focuses that differ from our own, simultaneously making them alien but also still vitally relatable.

Cleopatra had a very engaging voice as she tells us her life story. That of her family. What history has forgotten about her, what it has remembered, and what has been distorted. Of the people she met, how she shaped them and how they shaped her. It was really cleverly handled in regards to the relationship with Julius Caesar and also Mark Antony, with Saara El-Arifi really showing what a strong, magnetic character Cleopatra is.

I would have enjoyed more showing instead of telling, such as when we are told Cleopatra improved the economic situation of Egypt in her rule and uprooted corruption in her court. She would have stood out far more as a reader, I think, if we had been shown this instead of just told. But I do also understand there was so much to fit in this novel that showing everything would have resulted in a one-thousand page book.

Smooth writing, engaging characters, immersive details and a pace driven towards an ending we all expect and is referenced multiple times throughout the novel. A good palette cleanser!

3.75/5 STARS

April 30, 2026
2/5⭐️


Cleopatra.


Witch. Whore. Villain.


Queen.


This book follows Cleopatra’s story when she becomes queen, and all the series that follow her demise.

I think it had great potential to be amazing, and it’s all very quotable, but there’s a few things that held it back -for me, anyway.

I despised Cleopatra breaking the fourth wall, and foreshadowing EVERYTHING. She constantly broke it, just to spoil what would happen, right before it would happen! It was fine in the beginning, and almost added to the story, but that quickly changed once she started spoiling everything!!

The magic. Look, I love mythologies, Egyptian being one of them, but mixing magic into ACTUAL history, just messes with Cleopatra’s actual story. You didn’t need it. Especially with that insane ending.

Show not tell. There was so much telling and not enough showing. Don’t tell me she was the greatest Queen of all time, SHOW ME.

Her Lovers. We were constantly being told (by Cleopatra) that our historians got everything wrong, and that she was more than her lovers. Then the book proceeds to be mainly about her lovers, and withholding accurate details about them. (Like Cleo was in her 20s and Caesar was in his 50s). Not to mention both Caesar and Marcus were written so similarly, they were basically the same person.

Her naivety and “innocence”. We were told that she was incredibly smart, not once were we shown that, just told, but at the same time, she came across so incredibly naive, that she was almost borderline stupid. Also, making her not like death/killing, when in real life she killed anyone and everyone who stood in her way, was an interesting choice.

Like another reviewer said (I’m paraphrasing), trying to reclaim Cleopatras from a millennia of slander and Vilification, she has been completely defanged, and she’s now passive, and it feels like we’re going backwards instead of forward.

I would’ve preferred to see the smart, cunning, cutthroat, insane, Queen that she was, than the timid, naive, stupid, “queen“ That was portrayed here.

Note: honestly, I would’ve loved the magic elements, and the insane ending, had it been a fictional story!! That’s what hurts the most.

Thank you NetGalley, Random House Publishing Group, and Author for this digital ARC. All opinions are my own.

Having just finished Agrippa (5 stars BTW), I wanted to stay in the Classical era. Cleopatra looked like it would fit the bill.
It’s told from an odd perspective. Cleopatra is talking directly to the reader from beyond the grave. She makes constant remarks about what comes ahead, including her death. She also references how historians have depicted her.
But if you get beyond that, the story is told in a straightforward fashion. Well, until the end. I am not a big fan of magic realism and this version really didn’t work for me.
El-Arifi does an excellent job placing the reader in the time and place. I felt I was there - in the palace, on her barge, in the streets of Alexandria. She imparts the casual disregard for human life. She does a good job of capturing Cleopatra’s character - her worry over her lack of a divine power, her desire to be a healer, her concern for all of Egyptians not just the elite. But El-Arifi tries to capture a lot in 12 hours, so at times the story felt more broad brush than fine detail. Too much time is spent on her love of Julius Caesar and Marcus Antonius, when I would have preferred more on her attempts to rule. In fact, the book left me with the impression she did very little ruling.
I listened to this and I was less than impressed by Adjoa Andoh. Giving common Egyptians cockney accents really didn’t work. And her Italian accent for Caesar and Antonius was almost comical.

This was heartbreakingly beautiful! This was everything and more!

“I sought Cleopatra’s voice in the dust between tomes. And from the ancient stillness, she spoke back. This novel is not history, it is memory.” - What a way to start this story 👏🏼👏🏼

I instantly fell in love with Cleo’s story. We follow her from a young women how navigates loss and the responsibility of being a pharaoh, to adulthood. This is a story about motherhood, love and the perception of ancient Egyptian and western society on womanhood (which stills feels so relatable today, strange don’t you think?).

I feel like this book came at the perfect timing in my life. There are so many lesson I can learn. I’m going through it for the moment and what a book this is to keep me going.
El-Arifi has woven such a beautiful tale that I felt my heart break on multiple occasions. Cleopatra has always been such a head figure in our history books, but what do we actually know about her? Her story has been written and rewritten by so many accounts, it is hard to keep track of it. But this felt like a true rendition of her life, like an actuality and not just a perspective.

There are some quotes I would like to share with you. Without the full picture, it will most likely not make any sense, but these just stuck with me for some reason.

👀 “It is a reminder that not all roads lead to Rome. Let it not be the center of your history, for propaganda is a tool favoured by the West.”

💔 “Will we ever tire of men defining the parameters of womanhood? I look at the world as you live it, reader, an grow weary.”

💛 “You try to capture my essence but cannot, for you seek the truth in all the wrong places. ….. You will never define me, and that is the purest form of freedom I can hope to find in this life ….”

I will say that I absolutely loved the author’s note at the beginning of the book. This was the first book I read from El-Arifi, and I will be adding more to my tbr. I fell in love with her writing style and was immediately engaged with the characters!

I will recommend this book to anyone who will listen to me!

Narrated by Adjoa Andoh
Presented by Harper Collins UK Audio

Mixed but mostly negative feelings about the audio. I think she actually did a (mostly) brilliant job but it just wasn't for me.

The story itself was a bit disappointing to me, as I think it tried too hard to make her a sympathetic character. Cleopatra has always seemed like such a badass of history, and this rounds her out a bit more, but with tales of woe and hardship rather than steel. There's a huge focus on her as a mother and a lover, and I wanted more of her as a ruler. I guess that's kind of the point of the story - to offer the bits history doesn't - but to me it watered down the character into less than I expected.

I was also increasingly frustrated every time the story referred to things yet to come. While Cleopatra is such an iconic figure from history, I think there are many who don't know all the details of her life so it ends up spoiling a lot of big moments. I'm one of them - I know her as a badass queen but not too much about the details, and I was excited to learn more through this medium. So naturally, many of the references were big spoilers. I HATE SPOILERS. I'm the kind of person who doesn't even want to know how a book made you feel because it's a spoiler on how I might feel reading it.

I'm in two minds as to how I would go with the physical, compared to the audio. On the one hand, I think I would have appreciated Cleopatra as a person a little more, but I also think I would have been even more bored with the length of the story. This really does travel, giving plenty of detail of Cleopatra's life, and while it's nice to hear about everything, it does make it long and a little tedious at times. I enjoy audio for books like this, because I can zone out a little without missing much. But I always get a richer experience with reading physically so this may have led to a better impression of the character.

The narration itself was very hit/miss for me. I enjoyed the strength of her voice and its representation of the character, but at times it didn't seem to suit. Some of the pronunciations bothered me, and I felt sometimes it was a little more dramatic than necessary. But then at other times I was completely swept away by the performance, feeling true anguish when the character experienced it. I'd want to listen to this narrator on another book to see how it differs.

I did enjoy the story, but it didn't capture me quite as much as I wanted it to, and I wanted to hear more of the coldhearted queen of history. Still, it's stirred up more interest in researching the historical woman so that's never a bad thing! I'd definitely still encourage people with an interest in the Egyptian Queen to give this book a go.

With thanks to NetGalley for an audio ARC

I loved Saara El-Arifi's Faebound and Ending Fire series, so I was curious about her take on Cleopatra. Billed as historical fantasy, I'd call this more historical fiction, as there wasn't magic in it and it didn't have a lot of the hallmarks of fantasy. Even as historical fiction, this tale didn't quite work for me.

I did appreciate that it was a more sympathetic take on a woman who is painted as a power-hungry, cruel whore, showing Cleopatra instead as a mother, a passionate lover and a sensitive soul who wanted to be a scholar and healer instead of a ruler. But her legend soon overtook her even in life.

I didn't feel this was necessarily a Westernized take on her life, but I don't tend to care for biopics that are sweeping surveys of a life, and this was more of that. In covering her whole life, I felt it galloped from her love stories with her handmaiden Charmaine to Julius Caesar to Marcus Aurelius and her struggles to secure her rule. Too much time was spent on her alliance with Rome so that she almost felt like a vassal state instead of a ruler in her own right, despite the devotion of Aurelius and Caesar. I felt it should have focused on one time period of her life for me to feel more of an emotional connection to her life and loves. It also focused too much on her romances, but they were paced so quickly that as soon as I felt a connection to one then I was rushed off to the next.

I also found the constant foreshadowing annoying. Cleopatra is telling her legend in her own words and reclaiming her story, which I found an intriguing device, but in practice it meant a lot of telling and kind of snarky commentary about what was to come, and I started to find Cleopatra's arrogance annoying. This book did a good job of painting her as a complicated, yet sympathetic figure and humanizing the legend, but I just felt the pacing was too rushed for me to get really invested in the story.

I absolutely love this author and will read anything she writes, but this one was a miss for me.

Thank you to Netgalley and the publisher for the advance review copy. I am leaving this review voluntarily.

February 26, 2026
"YOU KNOW MY NAME.
BUT YOU DO NOT KNOW ME.

Your historians call me seductress, but I was ever in love's thrall.
Your playwrights speak of witchcraft, but my talents came from the gods themselves.
Your poets sing of my bloodlust, but I was always protecting my children.

How wilfully they refuse to concede that a woman could be powerful, strategic, divinely blessed to rule.

Death will silence me no longer.

This is not the story of how I died. But how I lived."

Where do I begin to share the genius of Saara El-Arifi's retelling of Cleopatra? This is the best one in my opinion. The author uses Cleopatra herself as narrator from beyond the grave to tell us her story. Not what we have learned over time that has been massaged by male historians to fit a narrative. One that labels her as witch, whore, and villian. We learn of her as daughter, sister, mother, friend, healer, scholar, and Pharoah.

The spellbinding tale begins when eighteen-year-old Cleopatra becomes Pharoah at the death of her father. The lush worldbuilding and vivid prose are completely immersive and atmospheric transporting the reader to ancient Egypt. I felt that I was watching a movie I was so completely captivated and able to picture what was happening. Cleopatra is fully fleshed out for us and we learn her innermost thoughts, dreams, and insecurities. It begins as a coming of age story but it is really a love story. Her love for Egypt, the goddess Isis, her siblings, friends, lovers, children and citizens. Her political alliances and strategies as well as mythical elements are seamlessly woven into the narrative to create a an epic story that is a mesmerizing read. I highly recommend for lovers of historical fiction infused with myth and legend.

Many thanks to NetGalley, Ballantine Books and Saara El-Arifi for the gifted advance reader's copy. All opinions are my own.
